rationale: The ask/seek/knock triad is close to word for word identical in both Gospels: "Ask, and it will be given to you; seek, and you will find; knock, and the door will be opened to you. For everyone who asks receives; he who seeks finds; and to him who knocks, the door will be opened" (Matthew 7:7-8, BSB) against Luke's "So I tell you: Ask, and it will be given to you; seek, and you will find; knock, and the door will be opened to you. For everyone who asks receives; he who seeks finds; and to him who knocks, the door will be opened" (Luke 11:9-10, BSB), which only adds the introductory "So I tell you." The father-and-son analogy that follows is where the two accounts checkably diverge. Matthew's pair of questions is bread-for-stone, then fish-for-snake (7:9-10, BSB); Luke's pair is fish-for-snake, then egg-for-scorpion (11:11-12, BSB) -- a different second pairing, not the same two images in a different order. The conclusion each account draws also differs in what is specifically promised: Matthew's is "how much more will your Father in heaven give good things to those who ask Him" (7:11, BSB); Luke's is "how much more will your Father in heaven give the Holy Spirit to those who ask Him" (11:13, BSB) -- a general "good things" against a specific, named gift. The type is parallel (two Gospel records of the same teaching, neither quoting the other by formula); the label is strong because both the near-verbatim triad and the specific points of divergence (the egg/scorpion pairing; "good things" against "the Holy Spirit") are directly checkable against each Gospel's own shipped BSB text, not an inference this connection is adding.
